notes_context:
Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0012] Verify money/state helpers against real models: Refund logic depends on Payment fields (amount, refunded_amount, status) and money helpers (to_money, round_money, ZERO); confirm their exact semantics before writing comparisons.
  Inspect models.py and money.py to confirm field names, Decimal vs float types, and rounding behavior, then compare rounded Decimals consistently (e.g. refunded + amount > payment.amount) and set status to 'refunded' only when the running total equals the captured amount.
- [rb-0009] Verify edge cases with a quick script after tests pass: Passing tests isn't enough; probe boundary inputs (exact boundary, before start, just-before boundary) with an ad-hoc script.
  After the test suite passes, run a short inline Python snippet exercising exact-boundary, pre-start, and off-by-one-second cases. This catches strict-vs-inclusive semantics bugs that a single happy-path test misses.
- [rb-0004] Match existing error codes and validation patterns before implementing: Grep the codebase for similar validation (state checks, amount checks) to reuse established BillingError codes and message formats.
  Before writing validation logic, search for existing patterns like `invalid_state` or `negative_amount` in sibling modules. Reusing the same error codes and f-string message formats keeps behavior consistent and satisfies hidden tests that assert on codes.
- [rb-0001] Reuse existing money helpers for Decimal math: When implementing monetary calculations, use the project's existing money utilities (to_money, round_money, ZERO) instead of raw Decimal arithmetic.
  Inspect ledgerly/money.py and models.py first to learn the money policy. Wrap inputs with to_money, seed sums with ZERO, and round results with round_money so rounding and type conventions match the rest of the codebase.
- [rb-0002] Guard division with a zero-total check: For weighted-average or ratio computations, check the denominator before dividing and return the documented fallback (ZERO) when it is zero.
  Compute total_quantity first; if it is falsy, return ZERO immediately. This satisfies the 'no lines means zero' requirement and avoids ZeroDivisionError without try/except.
- [rb-0003] Read the target module and tests before editing: Start by reading the file to be modified, related models/utilities, and any existing tests for the feature to align signatures and behavior.
  Cat invoice.py, models.py, money.py, and tests/test_average_unit_price.py before writing code. This reveals the exact stub signature, dataclass field names (line.quantity, line.unit_price), and expected return type, enabling a first-attempt pass.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw arithmetic
item.description: When implementing a pricing/money function, inspect the repo's money module and reuse its conversion and rounding helpers.
item.content: Before writing arithmetic, read sibling modules (e.g. money.py, payments.py) to find helpers like to_money/round_money and constants like ZERO. Using them keeps rounding and type handling consistent with the rest of the codebase and matches hidden-test expectations.

item.title: Match the project's error type and code conventions
item.description: Grep for existing raise statements to learn which exception class and code-string style the project uses before adding validation.
item.content: Validation errors should use the project's domain exception (e.g. BillingError(code, message)) with a short snake_case code, not bare ValueError, unless the surrounding module already uses ValueError. Grep for 'invalid_', 'non_positive', etc. to mirror naming.

item.title: Read the visible tests to pin down input/output types
item.description: Check tests and call sites to determine whether inputs are Decimal, float, or int, and what return type is expected.
item.content: A test like add_tax(Decimal('100.00'), 8) == 108 reveals Decimal inputs and numeric comparison. Normalize inputs through the project's money helper and return the rounded money type so equality checks pass.
